en: To the child born of your khan Manas?
You prepare poison for your own child;
Could anyone calling you a Muslim prosper?
Well, can there be a Muslim like you?
Without a post to tether a horse,
Such utter bareness is yours.
Giving poison to your own child,
Such infidelity is yours!
Can there be a Muslim like you?
Could anyone who calls you righteous prosper?
Through your hot temper, old man,
You became known as the swine khan.
Can there be a human like you?
Manas's only son Semetey,
That dear child found late in life—
How can you set upon him?
May this deed of yours come to nothing!
Let your six sons gather together,
And all be sacrificed for Manas alone!
When Manas lived,
I studied the words of the Haftiyak,
And rinsed my mouth with rich fat.
When my only one, Manas, passed away,
This hair of mine turned white.
When Manas the Leopard lived,
I was one who sliced belly fat.
Since Manas the Leopard passed away,
I have been despised worse than a Kalmyk.
When valiant Manas lived,
My wondrous treasury,
All my kinds of livestock were in readiness.
Over the eighteen thousand worlds
I used to stand as khan.
At the entrance to my door,
My tigers bred fifteen times.
No one dared approach.
There were sixty dragons,
And on this side of them
Stood elephants with sword-like trunks.
When Manas, blessed by Kydyr, lived,
Who else lived like this?
Since that Manas passed away,
Since he went to the next world,
Before your doorway
There is not a puppy, let alone a tiger.
For that son Manas,
Your children, the six wicked ones at their head,
Let them all be sacrificed!
When Manas lived,
We made merry in delight.
From all the different peoples,
Six thousand foals of barren mares apiece
We used to take as tribute.
Since that Manas passed away,
There is not a green ear of corn, let alone tribute.
Children worth less than a green ear,
Those half-made six wicked ones—
Can they be called children?
A wolf-maned man like Manas—
Can one who speaks of him like this prosper?
Can these be called children?
When my Manas lived,
Not a millet grain would fit in this mouth.
Since Manas passed away,
A calf's head fits it just right.
When my Manas lived,
Not a wheat grain would fit in this mouth.
When I look to the six wicked ones,
A bull's head fits it just right.
My Manas is gone; the sun is gone.
I see that the Night of Power is gone.
For a son like my Manas,
Let the Argyn people, the six wicked ones at their head,
All be sacrificed!
Mixing poison for your own child,
You commit the utmost wickedness.
If you keep doing this,
You will destroy your six sons!”
While the senior wife Bagdoolot spoke thus,
Khan Zhakyp stood gathering his fury.
Taking a hand-club in his hand,
He spoke, intending to inflict humiliation.
“When Khan Manas reached twenty long ago,
Untrodden by his Akkula,
Not one land remained.
Without hearing his roar,
Not one people remained.
When he raided the lower Urum people,
Crushing their khan,
Fighting and unleashing slaughter,
Wielding spears and breaking ranks,
Those whose death had come falling to bullets,
Slaughtering the Urum and taking gold coins,
Taking red-tailed elephants,
Taking gold loaded upon elephants,
Taking a thousand black-eyed girls,
When Manas seized the spoils,
When he slaughtered those people,
You were the one taken captive.
I was the one who received you as a gift.
Woman, you have wicked words of partiality from that time.
You, old woman, with Manas—
When he wished, you had been his lover.
I knew your wickedness.
Thinking of the words of old,
I suspected you were not innocent.
There is mischief in your mind.
From long ago, you cunning woman,
You had dealings with Manas.”
Thus he spoke and worked himself up,
Addressing his senior wife Bagdoolot.
The club in his hand
He gripped and swung,
And struck his wife upon the head.
Her head split, she doubled over;
Her strength failed, and the old woman
Fell headfirst to the ground.
Her strength drained; she grew faint,
Bleeding for as long as meat takes to cook.
“You wretched baldhead, you will never change!
Mixing poison for your own child,
You never give up your mischief!
Die yourself, not your child.
Die, you white-bearded old man!
Instead of striking me, let Abyke, Kobosh, all of you die!
You will wail, you baldhead.
Go and settle along the valley.
Instead of striking me, may all six of your sons die,
And may you be like a fire gone out!
You have been wicked from the start;
You are fit to become a dweller in hell.”
The senior wife Bagdoolot,
Her head split by the club,
Grieving in torment,
“Would that my mountain-like Manas had not died!
Would that no child had been left by Manas!
‘If his child comes, give him poison’—
O God, never lay that upon Your creatures!”
The senior wife grieved;
Her heart was sorely torn.
Tears poured from her eyes.
Her ribs seemed torn apart.
“He means harm to my child,” she thought.
The roaring old man
Seemed a devouring demon to his wife.
The senior wife rose and walked,
Stepped carefully into the pantry.
Large enough to fill six people,
That black bowl of Zhakyp's—
“Let the old man drink,” she thought,
And poured honey drink for Khan Bakai.
There was bozo in a leather bucket,
With burning poison mixed into it.
She poured poison for Semetey,
Mixed honey drink for Khan Bakai,
Mixed poison for your dear Semetey.
Long ago, when they raided Ombu and took spoils,
Attacked twelve cities,
And ravaged them,
The burning poison taken as booty
She now lifted with a spoon,
And put into the food to be served.
What splashed outside
Set the green grass blazing;
The earth burned fiercely.
Having readied the food,
The angry senior wife,
Unable to gather her wits,
Her heart sorely troubled,
The senior wife stood looking:
“Will he drink it?” she wondered.
Then the senior wife was dying with grief.
Khan Zhakyp had poison mixed.
Khan Bakai heard it all,
And raced on his gray steed.
To the orphan son of Manas
He galloped up.
“My tender gray-mottled falcon,
I have seen a thing of dreadful shape.
Listen, my gray goshawk, my morning star!
Today your grandfather, the swine khan, is your enemy.
Manas's son, you rascal,
Distress will be within you.
When he offers you his liquor,
If you drink it, you will die.
My orphan, you will see the next world.
You will perish in your youth.
My son, if you drink, you will not survive.
If you smell it, you will die.
Mark this well,
My son, how will you live then?
He poured honey drink for Khan Bakai;
I shall go and drink it down.
My son, he poured poison for you.
Drink if you wish; leave it if you wish.
If you are so hostile to your own life,
Drink it if you wish, orphan.
This Talas is no land for you;
Your grandfather, the swine khan, is no kin to you.
Weeping and wailing before you,
If he finds a way, that swine
Will put snuff into your eyes.
Weeping before you with ringing cries,
If he can, the swine khan
Will do you harm.
Beware of this, orphan.
Let us go to your grandfather, the swine khan.
If he has any friendly feeling,
Let us patiently watch for it.
Of the countless treasures left by your father Manas,
One portion is with him.
Let us ask your grandfather for it.
If he does not give it when asked,
Let us cast a cold lasso.
Come, my son Semetey,
Let us go to your grandfather, the swine khan.”
Showing him the Talas plain,
Khan Bakai brought
To Khan Zhakyp's home
The child left by Manas.
That orphan slave left by Manas,
Into his grandfather Khan Zhakyp's home,
The orphan entered radiantly.
His grandmother, the senior wife Bagdoolot,
When she saw Semetey,
Her dear quail-like eyes
Shed tears drop after drop.
Her dear eyes like currants
Shed tears a whip's length long.
Lamenting, weeping, crying out,
“The gift left by my kingly son Manas!” she said.
The senior wife wept and sobbed:
“Now grown old, Kanykei,
Is your mother still alive, my child?
Now grown old, Chyiyrdy,
Is your supporting kinswoman alive, my child?
Your renowned land of Talas,
Have you come safely seeking it,
And these Kyrgyz people of yours?
To Temir Khan's city
You wandered and grew up.
My ocean-like orphan, have you come?
To the walled city of Bukhara
You fled and grew up.
My supporting orphan, have you come?”
His grandmother Bagdoolot
Wept and sobbed over the boy.
“My orphan!” the senior wife cried,
Unable to contain her joy.
Seeing her orphan, the old woman
Stood lamenting and sobbing.
Khan Zhakyp, evil of heart,
His wickedness evident,
Falsely greeted the boy with ringing cries,
Merely pretended to weep and wail:
“My hoof left by the swift steed,
